goal: Close the two remaining instances of the RunState dt guard defect -- WaveScheduler.Tick and PlayerMotor.Tick both carry the identical `if (dt < 0f) throw ... "dt must be >= 0."` mismatch that WO-0008 fixed in RunState -- so that no Core type taking a dt parameter can be pushed into an unbounded loop or a silently poisoned state by a non-finite value. WaveScheduler's instance is the more severe of the two: it is a non-terminating loop with unbounded allocation, not a wrong number.
rationale:
Per PRO-0005 (qa-director, Studio/state/proposals/PRO-0005.json), this order reuses that analysis in full and does not re-derive it. Summary of the two failure modes, for context only:

WaveScheduler.Tick (Assets/Core/Spawning/WaveScheduler.cs:58-81): the guard at line 60 lets float.PositiveInfinity and float.NaN through. `_timeUntilNextSpawn -= dt` at line 70 with dt = +Infinity produces -Infinity; the `while (_timeUntilNextSpawn <= 0f)` loop at line 73 then never terminates, because `-Infinity + _interval` is still -Infinity on every iteration, and each iteration calls `into.Add(...)` -- a non-terminating loop with unbounded allocation into the caller's buffer, reachable from Assets/Unity/EnemySpawner.cs:45 on any frame that produces a non-finite Time.deltaTime. With dt = NaN, `NaN <= 0f` is false, so the scheduler silently stops spawning for the rest of the run instead.

PlayerMotor.Tick (Assets/Core/Player/PlayerMotor.cs:42-65): the identical guard at line 44 lets NaN and the infinities through. dt = NaN poisons `_fireCooldown` at line 60; `if (_fireCooldown < 0f)` at line 61 does not hold for NaN, so the NaN is retained; then TryFire's `if (_fireCooldown > 0f) return false` at line 80 is false for NaN, so the weapon fires on every subsequent call, permanently, at unbounded rate. NaN also propagates into PositionX through Clamp at line 58/89-96, since neither `x < _minX` nor `x > _maxX` holds for NaN, so it passes through unchanged and the player leaves the tracked bounds.

RunState.cs already carries the correct treatment (fixed under WO-0008, itself following PRO-0002): `if (!float.IsFinite(dt) || dt < 0f) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(dt), dt, "dt must be a finite number >= 0.")` at Assets/Core/Run/RunState.cs:70-73. This order applies the same predicate and the same message, verbatim, to the other two call sites, and extracts it into one shared helper so a fourth independent copy of this exact mismatch cannot be introduced by a future author who does not know the first three existed.

Shared helper: create `Assets/Core/DtGuard.cs`, namespace `MergeSurvivor.Core`, containing a single internal static class `DtGuard` with one method, `public static void RequireFiniteNonNegative(float dt, string paramName)`, whose body is exactly the condition-and-throw above, using the message "dt must be a finite number >= 0." character for character (matching RunState.Tick's current message exactly, so all guards in the codebase state the identical predicate in the identical words). WaveScheduler.Tick and PlayerMotor.Tick must call this helper as the first statement of Tick, before any other parameter validation or state mutation. RunState.cs is NOT required to be migrated to call this helper in this task -- it was already closed under WO-0008, its dispatched work order should not be silently reopened as a side effect of this one, and its current inline guard already states the identical predicate and message. If a future author wants RunState to call the shared helper too, that is a separate, trivial follow-up, not part of this order's scope.

CHA-0001 / RUL-0003 AUTHORISATION: qa-director's challenge CHA-0001 was upheld in full by ceo-orchestrator's ruling RUL-0003 (matter 1): the delivered guard leaves WaveScheduler.Tick's while loop non-terminating for large finite dt, because binary32 addition does not strictly increase its left operand once the addend falls below half an ulp of the accumulator (verified: with the default fixture Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f), Tick(1e8f, buffer) enters the loop and never leaves it, since `1f - 1e8f` and `1f - 1e8f + 2f` are bit-identical). RUL-0003 matter 2 refused both option (a) (compute the due-spawn count arithmetically instead of looping) and option (b) (narrow criterion 11's safety claim to the dt range over which the current loop happens to terminate), and ruled a third remedy instead: WaveScheduler.Tick must determine, before mutating `_timeUntilNextSpawn` and before appending anything, whether a due spawn's first catch-up increment would fail to strictly increase the post-subtraction timer, and if so must reject dt by throwing ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming dt, leaving `_timeUntilNextSpawn` unchanged and `into` untouched. RUL-0003 matter 2 explicitly authorises this: 'WaveScheduler.Tick may reject a finite, non-negative dt by throwing ArgumentOutOfRangeException when the resulting timer cannot be advanced by _interval in binary32. This is a change to the Tick contract and would otherwise contradict criterion 11 as currently written and trip WO-0010's escalateIf clause about callers depending on Tick's acceptance; it is authorised here, and the implementer may treat this ruling as the authorisation.' RUL-0003 also found, and this order records so the implementer need not re-derive it, that no existing caller is affected by the new rejection: Studio/sim/MergeSurvivor.Sim/Program.cs calls Tick only with 1f/30f, 1f/60f and 1f/240f, and Assets/Unity/EnemySpawner.cs passes Time.deltaTime; neither is anywhere near the rejection relation. Criterion 11 below is amended under RUL-0003 matter 3's authorisation and strictly on its terms: the safety claim is not narrowed, it is strengthened to be unconditional, and only the false justification and the inaccurate description of the accepted input set are corrected. The original text of criterion 11 as it stood before this amendment is preserved verbatim in CHA-0001's claim field so anyone checking later can confirm the amendment strengthens rather than narrows the safety claim. No other criterion of this order is touched by this amendment, by CHA-0001, or by RUL-0003.
acceptanceCriteria: A new file Assets/Core/DtGuard.cs defines `internal static class DtGuard` with `internal static void RequireFiniteNonNegative(float dt, string paramName)` that throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException(paramName, dt, "dt must be a finite number >= 0.") whenever `!float.IsFinite(dt) || dt < 0f`, and otherwise does nothing. The message string is character-for-character identical to RunState.Tick's current message.

WaveScheduler.Tick calls DtGuard.RequireFiniteNonNegative(dt, nameof(dt)) as its first statement, before the null check on `into`, before `_timeUntilNextSpawn -= dt`, and before any call to `into.Add(...)`. On the throwing path, `into` is left with exactly the same contents it had before the call (nothing appended) and the scheduler's internal `_timeUntilNextSpawn` is unchanged from its pre-call value.

PlayerMotor.Tick calls DtGuard.RequireFiniteNonNegative(dt, nameof(dt)) as its first statement, before the axis clamp and before PositionX or the fire-cooldown field are touched. On the throwing path, PositionX and FireCooldown are unchanged from their pre-call values.

WaveScheduler.Tick(float.NaN, buffer) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException, appends nothing to buffer, and a subsequent Tick with a valid finite dt spawns exactly as if the NaN call had never happened (same count and timing as an equivalent scheduler that never received the NaN call).

WaveScheduler.Tick(float.PositiveInfinity, buffer) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException, appends nothing to buffer, and a subsequent Tick with a valid finite dt spawns exactly as if the PositiveInfinity call had never happened.

WaveScheduler.Tick(float.NegativeInfinity, buffer) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException and appends nothing to buffer. (This case already throws today via `dt < 0f`; it must keep throwing under the corrected guard, and the acceptance test must note it is not a verdict-changing case the way NaN and PositiveInfinity are.)

PlayerMotor.Tick(float.NaN, 0f) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException; PositionX and FireCooldown are both finite and unchanged from their pre-call values; a subsequent TryFire call at any fire rate still respects whatever cooldown was in effect before the throwing call (it does not fire on every call from then on).
PlayerMotor.Tick(float.PositiveInfinity, 0f) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException with the same unchanged-state and cooldown-respecting guarantees as the NaN case above.

PlayerMotor.Tick(float.NegativeInfinity, 0f) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. (This case already throws today via `dt < 0f`; it must keep throwing under the corrected guard, and is not a verdict-changing case.)

The regression test for WaveScheduler's PositiveInfinity and NaN cases must be written so that it FAILS FAST against the unmodified pre-fix code rather than hanging the test run: use a test-only bounded IList<SpawnRequest> implementation (e.g. a small class local to WaveSchedulerTests.cs) whose Add throws a distinct exception type (not ArgumentOutOfRangeException) once its item count exceeds a small fixed cap such as 1000, and assert `Assert.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() => scheduler.Tick(float.PositiveInfinity, boundedBuffer))`. Against the unmodified code this must produce a fast, deterministic test failure (wrong exception type, because the loop runs past the cap before any ArgumentOutOfRangeException is thrown) -- not a hang and not a timeout. Against the fixed code it must pass quickly because the guard throws before the loop is ever entered. A test that relies solely on NUnit's [Timeout] attribute to abort a synchronous infinite loop is not acceptable, since that attribute does not reliably terminate a running thread on the runtime this suite executes under; the bounded-collection technique above (or an equivalent that fails fast rather than hangs) is required. State in the test's comment, in one sentence, which exception type and message the pre-fix run actually produces, as evidence that the failure is fast and deterministic rather than a hang.

[AMENDED per RUL-0003 matter 3, following CHA-0001; the original text of this criterion is preserved verbatim in CHA-0001's claim field.] The safety claim is universal and is STRENGTHENED, not narrowed: after this remedy, no finite input causes WaveScheduler.Tick to fail to return. Tick's XML doc comment together with the test suite must establish all four of the following about the schedule's catch-up advancement (today the `while (_timeUntilNextSpawn <= 0f)` loop at line 73; a corrected Tick may keep that shape, but these four clauses bind on whatever shape it now takes): (1) UNRESTRICTED TERMINATION -- for every dt that Tick accepts without throwing, the loop terminates in a finite number of iterations; no dt range is excluded from this claim. (2) CORRECTED, STATED JUSTIFICATION -- the original justification, that each iteration 'strictly increases _timeUntilNextSpawn by the fixed positive _interval', is false for binary32 addition (verified: with `_timeUntilNextSpawn` at `1f - 1e8f`, adding `2f` returns a bit-identical value) and must not appear, as though true, anywhere in the delivered code, its comments, or this order. In its place, Tick must reject, before mutating `_timeUntilNextSpawn` and before appending anything to `into`, any dt for which a spawn would be due (the post-subtraction timer is <= 0f) and adding `_interval` to that post-subtraction value would not strictly increase it. Tick's XML doc comment must state, correctly, why checking this once at the first prospective step suffices for every later step: `_timeUntilNextSpawn`'s magnitude is non-increasing across loop iterations, because each iteration adds the fixed positive `_interval` to a non-positive value, moving it toward zero; a non-increasing magnitude means a non-increasing ulp; so if the first increment strictly increases the timer, every later increment -- acting on a value of equal or smaller magnitude -- strictly increases it too. This invariant must also be pinned by a test, not stated only in a comment (see the stated-invariant test below). (3) EXACT REJECTION, NOT A THRESHOLD -- the rejected set is exactly the dt values meeting the condition in (2), determined by a direct comparison of the candidate post-increment timer value against the pre-increment value (e.g. compute the would-be next value and test whether it is strictly greater), never by a hard-coded or derived threshold constant such as a fixed multiple of `_interval`; a threshold constant would need re-deriving for every `_interval` the scheduler is ever constructed with and would silently drift out of correctness if it were not. (4) NO OVER-REJECTION -- a large finite dt for which the schedule can still genuinely advance (condition (2) does not hold for it) is accepted, not rejected, and Tick returns the full catch-up count for it, with every spawn that came due appended to `into`. This clause exists specifically to rule out an implementation that rejects any dt above some conservative fixed constant, which would satisfy clause (1) while defeating the scheduler's actual purpose. On the path where dt is rejected under (2), Tick throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming `dt`, leaves `_timeUntilNextSpawn` exactly at its pre-call value, and appends nothing to `into` -- the same throwing-path contract criterion 2 above already imposes for the DtGuard path.

The non-progress check required by amended criterion 11 is scheduler-specific -- a relation between dt-derived timer values and `_interval` -- and must live in WaveScheduler.Tick itself, not in DtGuard or any other shared helper. Folding it into DtGuard would conflate this defect class (a float-accumulation non-progress failure, CHA-0001) with the unrelated defect class WO-0011 is sweeping (a comparison-based guard that a non-finite value passes because the predicate omits a finiteness test), and the two must stay distinguishable in the code the same way they are distinguished in RUL-0003 matter 5.

On the path where WaveScheduler.Tick rejects dt under amended criterion 11 clause (2), the exception message states the predicate actually enforced -- that dt is too large relative to the scheduler's configured `_interval` for the schedule to advance -- and is textually distinct from DtGuard's "dt must be a finite number >= 0." message; the two guards enforce different predicates and must not read as though they enforce the same one.

This remedy makes no change to Assets/Core/Player/PlayerMotor.cs or to its tests beyond what criteria 3, 7, 8 and 9 above already require: CHA-0001 and RUL-0003 concern WaveScheduler.Tick only, and the PlayerMotor.Tick guard work in this order is unaffected by the amendment to criterion 11.

RATCHET TEST (RUL-0003 matter 4(i)) -- `Scheduler(firstDelay: 1f, interval: 2f).Tick(1e8f, boundedBuffer)` (using the BoundedSpawnRequestBuffer already in WaveSchedulerTests.cs) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming `dt`; `boundedBuffer` is empty afterwards; a subsequent `Tick` call on the same scheduler with a normal finite dt spawns exactly as if the rejected 1e8f call had never happened (same count as an equivalent scheduler that never received it). Do NOT use the form proposed in CHA-0001 -- asserting only that the call 'completes and returns a finite count' -- under any remedy: at dt = 1e8f with interval 2f, fifty million spawns are genuinely due, which exceeds BoundedSpawnRequestBuffer's cap of 1000 regardless of whether the loop terminates, so that form is red both before and after any fix, and its only 'green' path is widening the cap, which is a forbidden remedy in all but name. Evidence must show this test failing fast (in milliseconds, not a hang or timeout) against the pre-remedy code, with the actual output -- BoundedBufferCapacityExceededException at the 1000-item cap -- and passing after the remedy.

NON-OVER-REJECTION TEST (amended criterion 11 clause (4); RUL-0003 matter 4(ii)) -- a large finite dt that is well below the absorption relation for the scheduler's configured interval -- on the order of 1e5 seconds at interval 2f, chosen so the schedule provably still advances -- is accepted (Tick does not throw) and returns the full catch-up count, with every due spawn appended to the buffer. Without this test the ratchet above is satisfiable by an implementation that over-rejects, which is a second defect wearing the fix's clothes.

STATED-INVARIANT TEST (amended criterion 11 clause (2); RUL-0003 matter 4(iii)) -- a test pins the termination invariant itself, separately from the two boundary-value tests above, so that a future change silently reintroducing a non-terminating path is caught by a test and not only by a doc comment. Tick's XML doc comment must state the invariant and its justification in the terms of amended criterion 11 clause (2).

T3 EVIDENCE (RUL-0003 matter 4) -- a run of Studio/sim/MergeSurvivor.Sim at the same seed against the pre-remedy and post-remedy trees, with the resulting metrics.json compared field by field. No metric may move. If any metric moves, stop and escalate rather than adjusting anything: per RUL-0003, a moved metric would mean the ruling's monotonicity argument (that this remedy is behaviour-preserving for every dt on which today's code already returns) is wrong, and that must be reported immediately rather than reconciled.

The guard's condition and its exception message state the same predicate in both WaveScheduler.cs and PlayerMotor.cs, and that predicate matches RunState.Tick's, exactly as required when RunState was fixed: 'finite and >= 0' is what is checked, and the message says a finite number >= 0, not merely >= 0. (This is DtGuard's predicate only; it is distinct from, and unaffected by, the new non-progress check's own message required above.)

For every finite dt >= 0 that does not throw, WaveScheduler.Tick and PlayerMotor.Tick behave exactly as before this fix: all 9 existing tests in Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/WaveSchedulerTests.cs and all 9 existing tests in Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/PlayerMotorTests.cs pass unmodified, with no assertion in either file altered, weakened or removed.
RejectsNegativeDeltaTime (WaveSchedulerTests.cs) continues to pass unmodified: a finite negative dt still throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException under the new guard exactly as it did under the old one.
The full Assets/Tests/Core.Tests suite (all files, not only the two named above) builds and passes with DtGuard.cs, the corrected WaveScheduler.cs and the corrected PlayerMotor.cs in place.

Assets/Core/DtGuard.cs, Assets/Core/Spawning/WaveScheduler.cs and Assets/Core/Player/PlayerMotor.cs contain no reference to UnityEngine. WaveScheduler.Tick and PlayerMotor.Tick continue to take dt as an explicit float parameter rather than reading any ambient clock or Time.deltaTime.

Every new regression test required above (the NaN and PositiveInfinity cases for both types, at minimum) is demonstrated failing against the pre-fix WaveScheduler.cs/PlayerMotor.cs and passing after the fix, as WO-0008 criterion 7 required for RunState. Evidence must show the actual pre-fix failure output (exception type/message or assertion mismatch) for each, not merely an assertion that it would fail. The NegativeInfinity cases are exempt from this demonstration since they already throw pre-fix and are not verdict-changing.
escalateIf: Any assertion in an existing test file other than WaveSchedulerTests.cs or PlayerMotorTests.cs would need to change to make the suite pass

Any existing assertion within WaveSchedulerTests.cs or PlayerMotorTests.cs would need to be inverted or weakened to make the suite pass -- no inversion is authorised by this order, unlike WO-0008; if the implementer believes one is required, stop and escalate rather than treating this order as founder authorisation

A caller outside this task's write scope (e.g. Assets/Unity/EnemySpawner.cs or Assets/Unity/PlayerController.cs, or Studio/sim/MergeSurvivor.Sim/Program.cs) is found to depend on either Tick silently accepting a non-finite dt, such that rejecting it would break compilation or a documented external contract

The bounded-buffer regression test for WaveScheduler's PositiveInfinity/NaN case cannot be made to fail fast (in bounded time, without hanging) against the unmodified code, which would indicate the described hang is not reachable as specified

Migrating RunState.cs to call the new DtGuard helper turns out to be necessary to satisfy any criterion above (it should not be -- RunState's own inline guard already satisfies the predicate/message-consistency criterion on its own)
